{{Short description|Resolved problem in plane geometry}}
In [[Euclidean plane geometry]], the '''equichordal point problem''' is the question whether a [[closed curve|closed]] [[plane (geometry)|planar]] [[convex body]] can have two [[equichordal point]]s.<ref name="problems-geometry">{{citation
|author1=Victor Klee
|author2=[[Stan Wagon]]
|title=Old and New Unsolved Problems in Plane Geometry and Number Theory
|year=1991
|publisher=Mathematical Association of America
|isbn=978-0-88385-315-3
|url-access=registration
|url=https://archive.org/details/oldnewunsolvedpr0000klee
}}</ref> The problem was originally posed in 1916 by Fujiwara and in 1917 by [[Wilhelm Blaschke]], [[Hermann Rothe]], and [[Roland Weitzenböck]].<ref name="Blaschke">
W. Blaschke, H. Rothe, and R. Weitzenböck. Aufgabe 552. Arch. Math. Phys., 27:82, 1917
</ref> A generalization of this problem statement was answered in the negative in 1997 by Marek R. Rychlik.<ref name="The_Proof">{{citation
|author=Marek R. Rychlik
|title=A complete solution to the equichordal point problem of Fujiwara, Blaschke, Rothe and Weitzenböck
|journal=[[Inventiones Mathematicae]]
|year=1997
|volume=129
|issue=1
|pages=141–212
|doi=10.1007/s002220050161|bibcode=1997InMat.129..141R
|s2cid=17998996
}}</ref>

== Problem statement ==
An equichordal curve is a closed planar curve for which a point in the plane exists such that all [[Chord (geometry)|chords]] passing through this point are equal in length.<ref name="equichordal-point">{{citation
|author=Steven G. Krantz
|title=Techniques of Problem Solving
|publisher=American Mathematical Society
|year=1997
|isbn=978-0-8218-0619-7
}}</ref> Such a point is called an [[equichordal point]]. It is easy to construct equichordal curves with a single equichordal point,<ref name="equichordal-point"/> particularly when the curves are [[symmetric]];<ref name="symmetric">{{citation
|author=Ferenc Adorján
|title=Equichordal curves and their applications – the geometry of a pulsation-free pump
|date=18 March 1999
|url=http://web.axelero.hu/fadorjan/gepfdp/geopfdp.pdf
}}</ref> the simplest construction is a [[circle]].

It has long only been conjectured that no convex equichordal curve with two equichordal points can exist. More generally, it was asked whether there exists a [[Jordan curve]] <math>C</math> with two [[equichordal points]] <math>O_1</math> and <math>O_2</math>, such that the curve 
<math>C</math> would be [[star-shaped]] with respect to each of the two points.<ref name="problems-geometry"/><ref name="The_Proof"/>

== Excentricity (or eccentricity) ==
Many results on equichordal curves refer to their excentricity. It turns out that the smaller the excentricity, the harder it is to disprove the existence of curves with two equichordal points. It can be shown rigorously that a small excentricity means that the curve must be close to the circle.<ref name="Volkmer"/>

Let <math>C</math> be the hypothetical [[convex function|convex]] [[curve]] with two [[equichordal points]] <math>O_1</math> and <math>O_2</math>. Let <math>L</math> be the common length of all chords of the curve <math>C</math> passing through <math>O_1</math> or <math>O_2</math>. Then excentricity is the ratio

:<math>a = \frac{\|O_1-O_2\|}{L} </math>

where <math>\|O_1-O_2\|</math> is the distance between the points <math>O_1</math> and <math>O_2</math>.

== The history of the problem ==
The problem has been extensively studied, with significant papers published over eight decades preceding its solution:
# In 1916, Fujiwara<ref name="Fujiwara">M. Fujiwara. Über die Mittelkurve zweier geschlossenen konvexen Curven in Bezug auf einen Punkt. Tôhoku Math J., 10:99–103, 1916</ref> proved that no convex curves with three equichordal points exist.
# In 1917, Blaschke, Rothe and Weitzenböck<ref name="Blaschke"/> formulated the problem again.
# In 1923, Süss showed certain symmetries and uniqueness of the curve, if it existed.
# In 1953, G. A. Dirac showed some explicit bounds on the curve, if it existed.
# In 1958, Wirsing<ref name="Wirsing">E. Wirsing, Zur Analytisität von Doppelspeichkurven, Arch. Math. 9 (1958), 300–307.</ref> showed that the curve, if it exists, must be an [[analytic curve]]. In this deep paper, he correctly identified the problem as [[perturbation problem beyond all orders]].
# In 1966, Ehrhart<ref name="Erhhart">R. Ehrhart, Un ovale à deux points isocordes?, Enseignement Math. 13 (1967), 119–124</ref> proved that there are no equichordal curves with excentricities&nbsp;>&nbsp;0.5.
# In 1974, Hallstrom<ref name="Hallstrom">A. Hallstrom, Equichordal and Equireciprocal Points, Bogazici Univesitesi Dergisi Temel Bilimier-Sciences (1974), 83-88</ref> gave a condition on the curve, if it exists, that shows it must be unique, analytic, symmetric and provides a means (given enough computer power) to demonstrate non-existence for any specific eccentricity.
# In 1988, Michelacci proved that there are no equichordal curves with excentricities&nbsp;>&nbsp;0.33. The proof is mildly computer-assisted.
# In 1992, Schäfke and Volkmer<ref name="Volkmer">R. Schäfke and H. Volkmer, Asymptotic analysis of the equichordal problem, J. Reine Angew. Math. 425 (1992), 9–60</ref> showed that there is at most a finite number of values of excentricity for which the curve may exist. They outlined a feasible strategy for a computer-assisted proof. Their method consists of obtaining extremely accurate approximations to the hypothetical curve.
# In 1996, Rychlik<ref name="The_Proof"/> fully solved the problem.

== Rychlik's proof ==
Marek Rychlik's proof was published in the hard to read article.<ref name="The_Proof"/>
There is also an easy to read, freely available on-line, research announcement article,<ref name="The_Announcement">Marek Rychlik, The Equichordal Point Problem, Electronic Research Announcements of the AMS, 
1996, pages 108–123, available on-line at [https://www.ams.org/journals/era/1996-02-03/S1079-6762-96-00015-7/S1079-6762-96-00015-7.pdf]</ref> but it only hints at the ideas used in the proof.

The proof does not use a computer. Instead, it introduces a [[complexification]] of the original problem, and develops a generalization of the theory of [[Normally hyperbolic invariant manifold|normally hyperbolic invariant curves]] and [[stable manifold]]s to multi-valued maps <math>F:\mathbb{C}^2\to\mathbb{C}^2</math>. This method allows the use of global methods of [[complex analysis]]. The prototypical global theorem is the [[Liouville's theorem (complex analysis)|Liouville's theorem]]. Another global theorem is [[Algebraic geometry and analytic geometry|Chow's theorem]]. The global method was used in the proof of [[Ushiki's Theorem]].<ref name="Ushiki_Standard_Map_Theorem">S. Ushiki. Sur les liaisons-cols des systèmes dynamiques analytiques. C. R. Acad. Sci. Paris, 291(7):447–449, 1980</ref>
